title: Parables from Nature
sourceTitle: Parables from Nature (London: George Bell & Sons, 1882, 2 vols.; with the further parables from the G. P. Putnam's Sons edition, New York, 1880)
author: Margaret Gatty (Mrs. Alfred Gatty)
licenseEvidence: Public domain: Margaret Gatty died in 1873; first published in five series, 1855–1871. Scans used: George Bell & Sons, London, 1882 (University of Toronto copies on archive.org, vols. 1–2) and G. P. Putnam's Sons, New York, 1880 (Google scan on archive.org); all published before 1930. Not available on Project Gutenberg.
description: Margaret Gatty's beloved Victorian nature parables, a Charlotte Mason favorite: a caterpillar who learns faith from a lark, a robin who sings through a hard winter, a dragonfly grub wondering what lies above the pond, a spider exploring the 'empty space' of a church. Read a parable (or half of a long one) aloud, have your child tell it back, then draw, observe, or try a small experiment that matches it. Each tale carries a Christian lesson alongside real natural history, and the old illustrated editions are free to read online.
includes: 50 lessons in 7 units covering all 37 parables
Long parables split into 2–4 sittings; two very short ones paired
A narration prompt and a nature-study drawing, observation, or copywork step every lesson
Parent notes on sad moments, Victorian views, and the real science behind the stories
Links to the page where each reading starts in free scanned editions

units.title: Unit 1: A Lesson of Faith to A Lesson of Hope

lessons.title: Lesson 1: A Lesson of Faith
steps: Read “A Lesson of Faith” aloud together
Have your child tell the story back: the dying Butterfly, the worried Caterpillar, and the Lark's news
Draw the life cycle of a butterfly in four boxes: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly
questions: What did the dying Butterfly ask the Caterpillar to do?
What food did the Lark say the baby creatures would eat?
What did the Caterpillar find hatching from the Butterfly's eggs?
answers: Take care of her eggs and feed the babies dew and honey
Cabbage leaves
Little green caterpillars
lessons.notes: Gatty wrote these parables to teach Christian faith through nature; each opens with a Bible verse. This one pictures the hope of life after death, so be ready for questions.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: The Law of Authority and Obedience
steps: Read “The Law of Authority and Obedience” aloud together
Narrate the Traveller-bee's adventure: the dining room, the speech in the hive, and the quarrelling swarm
Draw a honeybee and label the queen, the drone, and the worker

links.label: Read “The Law of Authority and Obedience”

questions: What did the children say makes a bee grow into a queen instead of a worker?
Why did the runaway swarm get nothing done?
What did the old Relation want the Traveller-bee to see when they played at living together?
answers: The food the nurse-bees give it and the shape of its cell
They could not agree on anything because no one led them
That even two creatures living together need someone to lead and someone to follow
lessons.notes: This story argues for kings and against the idea that everyone should be equal, a common Victorian view. Older children can talk about whether they agree. The bee facts (queens raised by special food and cells) are accurate.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: The Unknown Land
steps: Read “The Unknown Land” aloud together
Ask your child to tell how the Mother Warbler answered her children's worries about leaving
On a world map, find Britain and Africa and trace the way small warblers fly south each autumn
questions: What is the 'Unknown Land' the Sedge Warblers sing about?
Who laughed at the young Warbler and told him there might be no such land?
What did the young birds do after their parents were shot?
answers: The faraway country where they will fly for the winter
A Magpie
They flew off to the Unknown Land on their own, trusting the call
lessons.notes: The parent birds are killed by a hunter near the end, which may upset sensitive listeners. The 'Unknown Land' is both bird migration and a picture of heaven.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Knowledge Not the Limit of Belief
steps: Read “Knowledge Not the Limit of Belief” aloud together
Narrate the argument between the Zoophyte, the Seaweed, and the Bookworm
Draw something seen through a magnifying glass or microscope, next to how it looks to the bare eye

links.label: Read “Knowledge Not the Limit of Belief”

questions: What did the Bookworm try to explain that the Seaweed and Zoophyte could not understand?
How did the Naturalist find out the Seaweed was a plant?
Why could the Bookworm never visit his two friends again?
answers: What seeing is
He dissolved its limy coat and looked at its fruit under a microscope
Their books were bound in Russia leather, and he hated the smell
lessons.notes: A good chance to talk about how scientists change their minds when they look more closely. Coralline seaweeds really are red algae, as the Naturalist decides.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Training and Restraining
steps: Read “Training and Restraining” aloud together
Narrate what the Wind told each flower and what the garden looked like after the storm
Look at a garden or houseplant that is staked or trained, and draw it with its support
questions: What did the Wind say was wrong with the way the Gardener treated the flowers?
What happened to the Convolvulus when her pole fell?
What did the young lady say she finally understood?
answers: He kept them tied up, clipped, and trained instead of letting them grow as they liked
Her flowers lay in the wet soil and were choked with mud
That people, like flowers, need training and restraint, or the garden turns into a wilderness

lessons.title: Lesson 6: The Light of Truth
steps: Read “The Light of Truth” aloud together
Narrate the four travellers who saw the Will-o'-the-Wisp and what happened to each
Draw a lighthouse and a Will-o'-the-Wisp side by side, each warning travellers away from danger
questions: What does the Will-o'-the-Wisp say its light is for?
Who took the light for his mother's lantern?
What did the Naturalist compare the Will-o'-the-Wisp to?
answers: To warn travellers away from the dangerous swamp
Little Colin, the farmer's son
A lighthouse that warns sailors away from rocks
lessons.notes: Two travellers (a statesman and a young woman) sink in the bog early in the story. Will-o'-the-wisps are faint lights over marshes, probably from burning marsh gas; scientists still are not completely sure.

lessons.title: Lesson 7: Waiting
steps: Read “Waiting” aloud together
Ask your child to tell the Mole's advice and the story of the young Ox's horns
Copy the Mole's saying “Everything will fit in at last” in your best handwriting
questions: Why was the House Cricket unhappy before there were houses?
Why did the young Ox keep butting everything with his head?
What finally made the Crickets happy?
answers: He loved warmth but had only cold, damp holes to live in
His horns were about to grow
The first fires on people's hearthstones gave them warm homes
lessons.notes: An Ape briefly suggests the crickets should kill themselves; the Mole talks them out of it. You may want to skip or soften that sentence for young listeners.

lessons.title: Lesson 8: A Lesson of Hope
steps: Read “A Lesson of Hope” aloud together
Narrate the argument between the Owl and the Raven during the storm
Draw the trees in the moonlight after the storm, with the Owl in his hollow
questions: What did the Owl keep calling the moon?
What did the Raven say was 'the law of life'?
How did the trees feel when the moon came out after the storm?
answers: The moon that shone in Paradise
Destruction
They were sorry they had doubted and were full of hope again
lessons.notes: The storyteller has just lost both parents; the story is a picture of hope in grief. The language is poetic, so pause to explain words like 'transitory' and 'revulsion'.

units.title: Unit 2: The Circle of Blessing, The Law of the Wood, Active and Passive

lessons.title: Lesson 9: The Circle of Blessing, part 1
steps: Read “The Circle of Blessing” from the start up to the drought on the mountain (p. 92)
Narrate the quarrel between the Sea and the Vapours, and where the trade-winds carried the Vapours
Draw the water cycle: sea, rising vapour, clouds, rain, and rivers running back to the sea, with arrows
questions: Why did the young man on the ship complain about the mists?
What did the Vapours leave behind in the Sea when they rose?
What happens to the Vapours when they reach cooler air high up?
answers: The hot, steamy calm near the equator made everyone miserable
Their salts
They cling together into drops, grow heavy, and fall as rain

lessons.title: Lesson 10: The Circle of Blessing, part 2
steps: Read “The Circle of Blessing” from the drought on the mountain to the end
Ask your child to follow the water's journey: rain, the Sundews, the Waterfall, the lake, the corn, the child's pinafore, and back to the sea
Add these stops to yesterday's water-cycle drawing, and copy the line “Small and great, great and small, we all depend on each other”

links.label: Read “The Circle of Blessing” from p. 92

questions: How did the Sundews keep their sparkling drops when the other leaves dried?
What keeps the lake in the park fresh and pure?
What did the Vapours leave behind in the caves when the Earth asked for something in return?
answers: Their sticky juices held the moisture longer
It gives out water through a stream at one end as it receives water at the other
Stalactites and crystals
lessons.notes: A lovely science reading: evaporation, trade-winds, condensation, groundwater, and stalactites are all here. Gatty ends with a line from the Benedicite hymn.

lessons.title: Lesson 11: The Law of the Wood, part 1
steps: Read “The Law of the Wood” up to “So things went on in the old way” (p. 111)
Narrate why the Birch and the Spruce-firs quarrelled
On a walk, find an evergreen and feel whether its inner branches are green or brown and dry
questions: What did the Spruce-firs shout when the Birch asked them to give way?
Why did the Wood-pigeons not want to nest in the fir grove?
How were the Spruce-firs hurting the Birch?
answers: “Never!”
They wanted more breeze and leafy shade than the thick, close branches gave
Their branches scratched off pieces of his papery bark

lessons.title: Lesson 12: The Law of the Wood, part 2
steps: Read “The Law of the Wood” from “So things went on in the old way” to the end
Narrate what became of the Spruce-fir grove and the one fir that survived
Copy the Birch's words “Mutual accommodation is the law of the wood”

links.label: Read “The Law of the Wood” from p. 111

questions: Why did the inside branches of the firs turn brown and dry?
Which tree did the Birch point to as an example of making room for others?
What happened to the last Spruce-fir?
answers: They grew so close that no fresh air could blow through
The Beech
It was made into a Christmas tree

lessons.title: Lesson 13: Active and Passive, part 1
steps: Read “Active and Passive” up to the sailor saying “Anyhow, boys, we'll watch” (p. 129)
Narrate what the Weathercock and the Dial each wished for, and what old Bowman noticed in the churchyard
Make a simple sundial with a stick in the ground and mark where its shadow falls each hour
questions: Why did the Weathercock envy the Dial, and why did the Dial envy the Weathercock?
What did the motto on the Dial's brass plate say?
Why was Bowman worried about the change of wind at three o'clock?
answers: The Weathercock wanted the Dial's rest; the Dial wanted the Weathercock's busy, useful life
“Watch, for ye know not the hour”
It came round with the turn of the tide and would blow a gale straight onto the shore all night

lessons.title: Lesson 14: Active and Passive, part 2
steps: Read “Active and Passive” from the night of the storm to the end
Narrate the rescue of the ship: who went out in the boat and how the village found out
Draw the shining Weathercock and the cleaned Dial, and copy the Captain's lesson: “Everything is useful in its place at the appointed time”
questions: What did the blue lights in the night mean?
Who was holding the helm of the ship all morning?
What reward did the Captain give the Dial and the Weathercock?
answers: A ship was in distress and calling for help
The old Captain from the Hall
He had the Dial's brass plate cleaned and the Weathercock gilded
lessons.notes: A tense shipwreck story with a happy ending. The title comes from Milton's line “They also serve who only stand and wait.”

units.title: Unit 3: Daily Bread, Not Lost but Gone Before, Motes in the Sunbeam

lessons.title: Lesson 15: Daily Bread, part 1
steps: Read “Daily Bread” up to the Tortoise disappearing into his winter bed (p. 158)
Narrate the Robin's talks with the Tortoise, the Blackbird, and the Woodlark
Draw the Tortoise's winter hole under the big stone, filled with leaves
questions: Why was the Tortoise cross with the Robin for singing?
What had the Woodlark noticed about every past winter?
Why did the Tortoise think the ground was a good place to sleep through winter?
answers: He was trying to go to sleep for the winter, and he thought there was nothing to sing about
Little bits of food always turned up somehow
It is much warmer under the ground than on the cold, damp surface

lessons.title: Lesson 16: Daily Bread, part 2
steps: Read “Daily Bread” from the snowstorm to the end
Narrate how the Robin kept singing and how he finally found food
Put out crumbs or seeds for winter birds this week, and copy the verse at the head of the story
questions: What happened to the holly berries the Robin had been eating?
Who heard the Robin's song and put out bread for him?
What did the Tortoise think of the Robin's story in the spring?
answers: Other birds ate them, and the gardener cut the last branches to decorate the house
The sad father who owned the house
He did not believe it and thought the Robin was telling travellers' tales
lessons.notes: The father is grieving his wife, who died on this day; the Robin's song comforts him. A good story to read near Christmas.

lessons.title: Lesson 17: Not Lost, but Gone Before, part 1
steps: Read “Not Lost, but Gone Before” up to the Frog saying “Go to rest, little fellow, and awake in hope” (p. 179)
Narrate the Grub's ride on the Frog's back and what the Frog saw on the bulrush
Look at a picture of a dragonfly nymph and an adult dragonfly, and draw them side by side
questions: What did the Dragon-fly Grub want to know?
What happened when the Grub's face came out of the water?
What did the Frog see climbing up the bulrush stalk?
answers: Where the Frog goes when he leaves the pond
He felt a terrible shock, fell back into the pond, and nearly died
A grub that split open and came out as a shining dragonfly

lessons.title: Lesson 18: Not Lost, but Gone Before, part 2
steps: Read “Not Lost, but Gone Before” from the Grub's promise to the end
Narrate the promise each brother made and why none of them came back
If you can, visit a pond on a sunny day and watch for dragonflies; draw one with its four wings

links.label: Read “Not Lost, but Gone Before” from p. 179

questions: What did the Grub promise his friends before he went up?
Why could the Dragon-fly never go back to tell them?
Who was waiting to welcome each new Dragon-fly?
answers: That he would come back and tell them if the great hopes were true
Touching the water gave him a deadly shock, so his wings carried him away
The ones who had gone before
lessons.notes: This is a parable about death and heaven: the ones who have died cannot come back to tell us, but they are “not lost, but gone before.” A gentle story for a child who has lost someone.

lessons.title: Lesson 19: Motes in the Sunbeam
steps: Read “Motes in the Sunbeam” aloud together
Narrate the game Kate and Undine played with the box
Shine a flashlight or let a sunbeam into a dim room and watch the dust sparkle; then copy “Sunshine is like love: it makes everything shine with its own beauty”
questions: What did the two girls try to catch in the box?
What did Undine first think the motes were?
Why does the dust look like stars, according to Mamma?
answers: The bright specks dancing in the sunbeam
Stars
Because the sun shines on it
lessons.notes: A short, quiet Christmas story. The hymn mentioned is “Christians, Awake, Salute the Happy Morn”; you might sing or listen to it together.

units.title: Unit 4: Red Snow to The Deliverer

lessons.title: Lesson 20: Red Snow, part 1
steps: Read “Red Snow” up to “But he was interrupted at last” (p. 11)
Narrate why Siegfried felt so sorry for Mont Blanc
Find the Alps and Mont Blanc on a map of Europe, and draw the snowy mountain with its rosy patch
questions: What did Siegfried see on the snow of Mont Blanc that he called a rose?
Why did Siegfried cry so hard in church?
What did the farmer's son say the pink snow was?
answers: A round, rosy-coloured patch
The pastor said the mountain was lifeless and God-deserted, like a hard, wicked heart
Red snow that sometimes falls out of the sky
lessons.notes: The pastor's sermon about people 'appointed to destruction' is harsh, and the story means it to be; the next part corrects it.

lessons.title: Lesson 21: Red Snow, part 2
steps: Read “Red Snow” from the stranger's arrival to the end
Narrate what the stranger showed Siegfried and his mother through the microscope
Draw the red snow plant as it looked under the microscope: tiny red balls, some splitting into four or eight
questions: What was the red colour on the snow really?
How does one red snow plant make new ones?
What did Siegfried grow up to become?
answers: Millions of tiny plants growing in the snow
Its red inside divides into small balls that grow, burst out of the cell, and start new plants
A pastor who never gave up hope for anyone
lessons.notes: Red or 'watermelon' snow is real: it is caused by tiny algae and can still be seen on high mountains in summer. You could look up photographs together.

lessons.title: Lesson 22: Whereunto?
steps: Read “Whereunto?” aloud together
Narrate what each creature (Star-fish, Limpet, Sea-mat, Coralline, and the Sea) said the tangle was for
Draw a big oarweed (kelp) plant with some of the creatures living on and around it
questions: How did the gloomy visitor accidentally save the Star-fish?
What does the blue-eyed Limpet use the tangle for?
What did the great Sea roar that sea-weeds are for?
answers: He flicked her with his stick into the shade of the tangle
As her home and her food
To keep the sea pure, sweet, and healthy by taking in bad vapours and giving out good ones
lessons.notes: Each creature thinks the seaweed exists just for it, which is the joke. If you live near a rocky shore, visit at low tide to look for kelp, limpets, crabs, and starfish.

lessons.title: Lesson 23: Purring When You're Pleased
steps: Read “Purring When You're Pleased” aloud together
Narrate how the two kittens were different and what happened when the children chose them
Draw Puss Missy and Puss Master, and copy the title as a reminder to say thank you
questions: Why did the mother cat scold Puss Missy?
Why did the boy choose Puss Missy?
Why was the pale little cousin so quiet and unsmiling?
answers: For purring and showing thanks so freely, which she thought was beneath her dignity
Because she purred when she was pleased
Her parents had died, and her strict guardian had taught her to hide her feelings
lessons.notes: A sweet story about thankfulness and about a grieving child who learns to show her feelings again.

lessons.title: Lesson 24: The Voices of the Earth
steps: Read “The Voices of the Earth” aloud, pausing to explain hard words
Ask your child to tell what made the Wind so unhappy and how the Earth answered each complaint
Over a day, list the happy and thankful sounds you hear (laughter, birdsong, a thank-you) that the Wind would carry
questions: Why did the Wind wish it could stop blowing?
What happy sounds did the Earth say outnumber the sad ones?
What did the Earth and the Wind agree to at the end?
answers: It had to carry people's curses, cries, and sins as well as their prayers
Healthy breathing, children's laughter, happy love, and everyday thanks
The Wind would keep working as long as good outweighs evil in the world
lessons.notes: This is the most abstract parable in the book: a poetic dialogue with no plot. For younger children, read it slowly in two halves or simply talk about the idea of the wind carrying our words.

lessons.title: Lesson 25: The Master of the Harvest
steps: Read “The Master of the Harvest” aloud together
Narrate the year of the wheat: drought, rain, weak plants, storm, too much rain, and harvest
Draw a stalk of wheat at three stages (green blade, flowering ear, golden ripe ear), or plant a few wheat or grass seeds and watch them sprout
questions: What did the Master of the Harvest do every time the weather went wrong?
What did his wife write in the back of her Bible?
How did the farmer change after reading her Bible?
answers: He grumbled and complained
A Bible verse, the date, and a short prayer each time
He stopped complaining and grew patient and hopeful like her
lessons.notes: The farmer's wife is ill throughout and dies before the harvest is gathered. The story is about patience and about God's patience with us.

lessons.title: Lesson 26: The Deliverer
steps: Read “The Deliverer” aloud together
Ask your child where the different people expected the Deliverer to be born, and where He really came
Copy the names from Isaiah: “Wonderful, Counsellor, The Mighty God, The Everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace”
questions: Where did most people expect the Deliverer to be born?
What did the wise men and philosophers hope He would be?
Who first heard the news of His birth?
answers: In a king's palace
A great teacher of reason and wisdom
Shepherds watching their flocks at night
lessons.notes: A Christmas meditation rather than a nature story. Good to read during Advent alongside Luke 2.

units.title: Unit 5: Inferior Animals to Night and Day

lessons.title: Lesson 27: Inferior Animals, part 1
steps: Read “Inferior Animals” up to the heading “What the Rook Says” (p. 88)
Narrate what the storyteller wonders about as he hides by the hedge and watches the rooks
Watch a flock of crows, rooks, or other birds for ten minutes and write down everything they do
questions: What are the rooks doing in the field?
What job does the rook in the tall oak have?
What can a dog do that its master cannot explain?
answers: Meeting in a great crowd, hopping, pecking, and cawing
He is a sentinel who keeps watch and warns the flock of danger
Find his way home by a short cut he has never taken, or bring back exactly the stone his master threw

lessons.title: Lesson 28: Inferior Animals, part 2
steps: Read “Inferior Animals” from “What the Rook Says” to the question “By what possible means could birds ever degenerate into men?” (p. 97)
Narrate the Rook's reasons for thinking men are not better than rooks
Make a two-column chart: things birds can do that people can't, and things people can do that birds can't
questions: What did the Rook say proves rooks are better than men?
What surprising idea did the Rook announce about where men came from?
What did the Rook imagine had happened to the young rooks that men shot and carried away?
answers: Rooks fly, have warm feathers, and are content; men walk lop-sidedly, need clothes, and are always restless
That men were once rooks who lost their wings
That they were living with men as their honoured teachers

lessons.title: Lesson 29: Inferior Animals, part 3
steps: Read “Inferior Animals” from p. 98 to the end
Narrate the Rook's 'proofs' from Mr. Raven-wing, Mr. Yellow-beak, and Mr. Grey-legs, and how the dream ended
Draw one of the Rook's 'proofs' (a chimney, a chimney-sweep, or a balloon) as the Rook saw it
questions: How did the Rook explain that men lost their wings?
What did Mr. Yellow-beak think the tall brick chimneys were for?
What was the storyteller doing when he woke from his dream?
answers: By walking on the ground for ages until their unused wings shrank into arms
Trees that men would one day roost in
Lying by the hedge, with the field empty and the rooks gone
lessons.notes: Written in 1861, two years after Darwin's 'Origin of Species', this is Gatty's satire of evolution theories: the Rook builds a grand theory from guesses. One passage refers to dark-skinned people in a way that reflects Victorian attitudes; you may want to skip it or talk about it.

lessons.title: Lesson 30: The General Thaw
steps: Read “The General Thaw” aloud together
Narrate the quarrel between the Ice, the Water, and the Snow, and how it ended
Put a piece of ice and a spoonful of snow (or frost from the freezer) in a cup and watch them all turn to water; draw before and after
questions: Why did the Ice think he was so important?
How did the skaters get rid of the Snow that covered the Ice?
What did the Ice, Snow, and Water discover when the thaw came?
answers: The skaters and sliders admired him, so he thought it was all in his honour
They had men sweep and shovel it into heaps at the sides
That they were all brothers, made of the same water
lessons.notes: The last line says the 'general thaw' that makes brothers of us all is death; you may want to talk about why it is better to make peace sooner.

lessons.title: Lesson 31: The Light of Life
steps: Read “The Light of Life” aloud together
Narrate everything Hans did for his rose-tree, and what he forgot
Start an experiment: sprout two pots of seeds, one in a dark cupboard and one on a sunny sill, and compare them in a week
questions: What did the nursery gardener say makes roses beautiful?
Why did Hans's rose-tree die?
What did the gardener say God's grace is for a person?
answers: Bones, hair, and soap-suds as manure
He boarded it in so carefully that it never got any light
What sunlight is for a plant: the main thing it needs to thrive
lessons.notes: Hans is described with old words for a person with an intellectual disability. The story treats him kindly; you may want to explain that we use different words today.

lessons.title: Lesson 32: Gifts
steps: Read “Gifts” aloud together
Narrate what each vegetable boasted about, and what the Rain-drops told them
Pull or buy a carrot, radish, onion, and beet; cut each open and draw what you see inside
questions: Why were the Cress and the Mustard so unhappy?
What did the Rain-drops say about every plant?
What happened to the Carrot that tried to stop growing down?
answers: They grew only little fibres instead of big roots like the others
Each one is good after its kind and has its own part to play
It grew into a thick, crooked lump and was only good for soup
lessons.notes: Based on 1 Corinthians 12, “there are diversities of gifts.” A gentle story for a child who compares himself with a sibling.

lessons.title: Lesson 33: Night and Day
steps: Read “Night and Day” aloud together
Narrate the quarrel between Night and Day and what they learned at the Poles
In a dark room, shine a flashlight on a globe or ball and spin it slowly to show how day and night really happen; find the North and South Poles
questions: In the old northern tales, what were the names of the horses of Night and Day?
What did Day wish would happen?
What did Night and Day find at the Poles, where each rules for six months?
answers: Frosty-mane and Shiny-mane
That he could go on forever with no night at all
Ice and rock, with almost no life at all
lessons.notes: The horses come from Norse myth. Gatty ends by explaining the real cause of day and night, the spinning earth.

units.title: Unit 6: Kicking to Birds in the Nest

lessons.title: Lesson 34: Kicking, part 1
steps: Read “Kicking” up to Firefly saying he will go on kicking out of spite (p. 170)
Narrate how Firefly was caught and what the old mare Egeria told him
Draw a horse's bridle and halter, and label the bit, reins, and headstall
questions: How long had Firefly lived free in the fields before he was caught?
How did Egeria say colts are raised in the East, where her mother came from?
What did Firefly decide he would do?
answers: Three years
They live among the tents and are fed and petted by the women from the start, so they are not afraid of people
Kick, kick, kick

lessons.title: Lesson 35: Kicking, part 2
steps: Read “Kicking” from p. 170 to where Whitefoot and Silverstar have gone to good homes (p. 178)
Narrate the difference between Taffy's advice and Egeria's, and how the three colts took their training
Copy Egeria's warning: “Those who indulge themselves in kicking at all, will sometimes kick when they would give worlds to forbear”
questions: Who gave Whitefoot and Silverstar good advice?
What hard things did the colts have to learn to bear?
Why did Egeria warn Firefly about kicking 'with a reason'?
answers: Taffy, the old Welsh pony
The iron bit in their mouths, the bridle, and going round in circles under the whip
Because kicking would become a habit he could not stop even when he wanted to

lessons.title: Lesson 36: Kicking, part 3
steps: Read “Kicking” from p. 178 to the end
Narrate Firefly's masters one by one, and what finally cured him
Talk together: when is it hardest to obey? Then draw Firefly standing still beside his young mistress
questions: Name two of the masters Firefly had before the clergyman's daughter.
What terrible thing happened on the Downs?
What did the young lady ask her father to do with Firefly?
answers: A young squire, a country doctor, and a horse-dealer
Firefly kicked and threw his kind young mistress, and she lay stunned on the ground
Send him to Rarey to be cured
lessons.notes: John Rarey was a famous American horse-tamer of the 1850s. The closing list of obediences (including 'wives under husbands') reflects Victorian views; you may want to talk about it with older children.

lessons.title: Lesson 37: Imperfect Instruments, part 1
steps: Read “Imperfect Instruments” up to Geronimo's idea of a festival for his father's birthday (p. 203)
Narrate the quarrel over Geronimo's mother's memorial tablet and how the village took it
Find Wales on a map of Britain, and draw the little church with its tower in the valley
questions: What did Geronimo want to move, and why was it so hard for his father?
Why would Roger the mason not do the job?
What did Geronimo plan in order to bring the village together again?
answers: The marble tablet in memory of his mother, which his father loved to look at every Sunday
He thought it would break the old man's heart to take down his own wife's stone
A festival with music and a supper on his father's birthday
lessons.notes: This is a story about a stubborn young clergyman, written mostly for grown-ups. Younger children may enjoy it more if you tell the first half in your own words and read the organ-tuning part aloud.

lessons.title: Lesson 38: Imperfect Instruments, part 2
steps: Read “Imperfect Instruments” from p. 203 to the end
Narrate what went wrong when Geronimo tuned the organ himself, and what the organ-builder explained
Fill glasses with different amounts of water, tap them, and try to tune two of them to sound sweet together
questions: Why did Geronimo try to tune the organ himself?
What happened when he played Haydn's Mass after tuning it?
Why did the organ sound wrong, according to the organ-builder?
answers: The organ-builder was away and he wanted it perfect for the festival
The chords clashed into horrible discords
He had tuned it too perfectly; an imperfect instrument needs some notes left a little flat or sharp
lessons.notes: This is real music science: to make every key sound good, organs and pianos are tuned with some intervals slightly 'off' (called temperament).

lessons.title: Lesson 39: Cobwebs
steps: Read “Cobwebs” aloud together
Narrate Twinette's three trips down her 'family rope' and what she met each time
Find a spider web outdoors (early morning dew makes them easy to see) and draw it carefully, thread by thread
questions: What did Twinette's mother say she should look for before spinning a web?
What three things surprised Twinette on her trips down?
How many eyes does Twinette have?
answers: Empty space below, for flies to fly in
A dazzling sunbeam, a gust of wind, and the darkness of night
Eight
lessons.notes: Gatty's description of the spider's silk (several spinnerets twisting fine strands together) is accurate. The ending pokes gentle fun at people who think they have figured everything out.

lessons.title: Lesson 40: Birds in the Nest
steps: Read “Birds in the Nest” aloud together
Narrate each time the hen-mother thought she was 'perfectly happy', and what came next
Draw the nest with eight eggs, then the eight young birds flying out into the wood
questions: How many eggs were in the nest?
Why did the hen-mother come to like night better than day?
What did she finally learn about being happy?
answers: Eight
At night all her young ones came back to the nest
That rejoicing in her children's joy, and loving the whole wood as a larger nest, made her happiest
lessons.notes: A tender story for parents as much as children, about letting children grow up. This is the last parable in the 1882 Bell edition; the remaining eight are read from a different scan (see the next unit).

units.title: Unit 7: The Later Parables, Consequences to Unopened Parcels

lessons.title: Lesson 41: Consequences, and The Cause and the Causer, part 1
steps: Read the short parable “Consequences”, then “The Cause and the Causer” up to “But the professor was gone too!” (p. 171)
Narrate where the stone's ripples went, then how the insects began their inquest on the dead moth
Drop a pebble into still water and watch the rings spread; draw them
questions: What did the stone shout as it sank to the bottom of the pond?
What did Dr. Earwig find stuck to the dead moth's proboscis?
Where had the bumble-bee picked up the same kind of 'foreign body'?
answers: “There an end!”
Several little sticky 'foreign bodies'
Inside an orchis (orchid) flower
lessons.notes: “Consequences” is only two pages: a small lesson that our words and deeds spread like ripples. “The Cause and the Causer” is set up as a courtroom inquest among insects; enjoy the funny characters.

lessons.title: Lesson 42: The Cause and the Causer, part 2
steps: Read “The Cause and the Causer” from Dr. Earwig climbing into the orchid to the end
Narrate what Dr. Earwig saw inside the orchid, and the three different opinions given at the inquest
Look closely at a flower (any kind) with a magnifying glass, find the pollen, and draw where it sits

links.label: Read “The Cause and the Causer” from p. 172

questions: What were the 'foreign bodies' really?
Why do orchids need insects to carry their flower-dust?
What did Sir Helix the Snail decide was behind this clever plan?
answers: Little packets of flower-dust (pollen) with a sticky ball at the end
The flower cannot dust itself, because its pollen sits too far from the sticky spot that needs it
A great unseen Intelligence who designed it
lessons.notes: The orchid facts come from Darwin's 1862 book on orchid pollination, and they are accurate (even the pollen-packet bending down after it is picked up). Gatty uses them to argue for a Creator; Bumble major and Bumble minor speak for chance and for evolution.

lessons.title: Lesson 43: Ghosts
steps: Read “Ghosts” aloud together
Narrate how the Draught talked the Fire into breaking out, and what became of the Fire
Talk about fire safety at home: find your smoke alarms, the fire guard or screen, and your family's meeting place outside; draw a map of how you would get out
questions: What was the brass guard in front of the grate for?
Who told the people at supper that the ball-room was on fire?
What finally put the Fire out?
answers: To keep sparks and burning coals in, and the ladies' dresses away from the fire
The Smoke
Barrels of water from the pond
lessons.notes: The 'ghosts' are Gatty's playful name for the invisible gases in fire and air. One simile compares the flames to 'Indians after their prey', a phrase of its time you may want to skip.

lessons.title: Lesson 44: These Three
steps: Read “These Three” aloud together
Narrate the Moss's journey: the broken flower-pot, the terrace walk, and the tombstone
Find moss growing on a wall, stone, or tree; look at it closely with a magnifying glass and draw it, then copy “And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three”
questions: What did the Moss always say as it crept onto something new?
What words did the granddaughter write under her drawing of the moss-covered flower-pot?
What did the Tombstone keep saying, and what did the Moss answer?
answers: “By your leave”
“Life in death. CHARITY.”
“I belong to Death”; the Moss answered, “And I to Life”
lessons.notes: The old rector and his wife die and are buried in this story, told very gently. The title and closing text come from 1 Corinthians 13: faith, hope, and charity (love).

lessons.title: Lesson 45: The Universal Language and See-Saw
steps: Read “The Universal Language” and the short parable “See-Saw” aloud together
Narrate who heard the Nightingale's song and how it comforted each one; then tell what the Snail said to the grumbling Oak
Make a see-saw with a ruler balanced on a pencil and two coins; find where the middle has to be to balance
questions: Which homesick plants in the kitchen-garden listened to the Nightingale?
What words did the Nightingale's song always end with?
What did Sir Helix the Snail tell the Oak his job was?
answers: Foreign plants such as the Portugal Onion, the Tomato, the French Beans and Marrows, and the Peach
“The same sun by day, the same moon by night, stars watching above”
Holding both ends of the see-saw up, steady in the middle, which the children could not do for themselves
lessons.notes: The 'universal language' is sympathy, which everyone understands without words. In this scan the last three words of “The Universal Language” are missing; the sentence ends “...and Love, are one.”

lessons.title: Lesson 46: A Vision
steps: Read “A Vision” aloud together
Narrate the walk to church on the spring morning, and why the storyteller wanted to leave the old church
Draw pink almond (or other) blossoms against a blue sky, the sight the storyteller loved
questions: What flowering trees did the storyteller want to see on the way to church?
Why was the storyteller annoyed when sitting in the old church?
What words from the service brought comfort?
answers: Almond trees
It was the wrong church, with ugly old box pews and tablets instead of the beautifully restored one
“When the wicked man turneth away from the wickedness that he hath committed... he shall save his soul alive”
lessons.notes: A reflective story for older children about going to church with the right heart; it quotes the Book of Common Prayer. Younger children may simply enjoy the spring walk.

lessons.title: Lesson 47: Unopened Parcels, part 1
steps: Read “Unopened Parcels”, Part I
Narrate the excitement of the parcel from the old home, and what Honor found inside her walnut
Copy the motto at the top of the story: “Judge not the play before the play is done”
questions: Who sent the parcels from the old home?
Why was Honor disappointed at first?
What was hidden inside the walnut shell?
answers: Grandmamma
Her little parcel seemed to hold only a common walnut
A fine, soft kid glove

lessons.title: Lesson 48: Unopened Parcels, part 2
steps: Read “Unopened Parcels”, Part II
Narrate the 'unopened parcels' Honor's father talked about: arithmetic, the Catechism, and the walnut itself
Crack open a walnut, find the tiny germ between the halves, and draw it; if you can, plant a nut or seed and watch for it to sprout
questions: How did arithmetic help sailors, according to Honor's father?
What 'parcel' did old John open when he wanted to come to Communion?
Why did Papa say a plain walnut is more wonderful than the glove?
answers: They use calculation to find their way across the pathless ocean
The answer from the Catechism he had learned as a boy
Its tiny germ holds a whole walnut tree

lessons.title: Lesson 49: Unopened Parcels, part 3
steps: Read “Unopened Parcels” from Part III to “And now comes the kernel of my story” (p. 264)
Narrate how Honor's father was saved from drowning at school, and what he thought of the boy who saved him
Talk about water safety: why swimming beyond the safe limits is dangerous
questions: What book did Grandmamma send Honor two years later?
How did Honor's father nearly drown?
What did his own father tell him about winning his hero's friendship?
answers: Longfellow's poems
He swam out beyond the safe bounds, a current carried him away, and he got a cramp
That he would have to deserve it

lessons.title: Lesson 50: Unopened Parcels, part 4
steps: Read “Unopened Parcels” from p. 264 to the end
Narrate the hero's old secret and how his friend helped him
Copy Tennyson's lines “That men may rise on stepping-stones / Of their dead selves to higher things”
questions: What had the hero done as a little child that troubled him for years?
Who turned out to be the hero?
What did his mother say when he finally told her?
answers: He let everyone believe he had seen his dead father's ghost
Honor's Uncle Frederick
That she had suspected it for years, and to kiss her
lessons.notes: A long story for older children about owning up to a wrong, and how even a fault repented of can make us better. The last of the parables.
